opus-5.5.text:
You know, I think every scientist I know got into science because of exactly those questions. When you're five or six, you ask: why am I me and not someone else? What happens when I fall asleep? Where was I before I was born? Is the red I see the same red you see? And then at some point most people stop asking, not because they found the answers, but because life gets busy and the questions start to feel childish.

For me, neuroscience was a way of being allowed to keep asking them, professionally. And what changed is not that I got answers. It's that the questions got sharper. As a kid you ask, "What is a thought?" As a neuroscientist you can actually sit next to a patient with electrodes in their brain, watch individual neurons fire when they think about a specific person or a specific memory, and ask, "Okay, is *this* the thought? Or is this just the thought's footprint?" That's a much better question than the one I started with, but it's not an answer.

The other thing that changed is humility. When you study the brain, you realize how much of what you experience as "you deciding" is actually happening before you're aware of it. That reframes things like free will, responsibility, even who I am. The child in me wanted certainty, a clean answer. The scientist in me has learned to be comfortable living inside the question, and honestly, to enjoy it more. The wonder didn't go away. If anything, knowing how a hundred billion neurons pull off the trick of making me feel like a single person sitting here talking to you makes it more astonishing, not less.

So I'd say science didn't replace the big questions. It gave me better tools to keep asking them, and it taught me that "I don't know yet" is a perfectly respectable place to live.

r001.rationale: The candidate says science let the speaker keep asking childhood questions and sharpen them, but explicitly says it did not provide answers. It does not describe beginning to answer questions previously dismissed as unanswerable.

fable-5.1.text:
You know, when I was a kid, the questions were all the obvious ones. Why am I here? What happens when I die? Is there a God? Why do I feel like me and not like someone else? And I think most kids ask those, and then at some point life gets busy and you stop asking. What's funny about becoming a neuroscientist is that I never really stopped. I just got better tools.

So the biggest shift for me is that science didn't answer the childhood questions, it changed what the questions are. Take "who am I?" As a kid that feels like a mystery with one answer, like there's a little Moran sitting inside my head. Then you spend years recording from single neurons in people's brains, patients with epilepsy who let us listen to individual cells, and you watch a memory get formed or a decision get made before the person is even aware they made it. And you realize the "I" is not a thing, it's a process. It's a story the brain tells after the fact. That doesn't make the question less interesting. It makes it stranger, and honestly more beautiful.

The other thing science did is it made me comfortable with not knowing. When you're a child, uncertainty is scary. You want the adult to give you the answer. In the lab, uncertainty is the whole job. You live in it. And I think that's a healthier relationship to the big questions. I don't need to know what happens when I die to be at peace with it. I know roughly what happens to the neurons. I know that consciousness, as far as we can measure it, is something the brain does rather than something it has. Whether there's anything beyond that is a question science can't currently reach, and I've learned to say "I don't know" without anxiety.

And then there's the humbling part. The more you study the brain, the more you see how much of what you believe about yourself is just a convenient narrative. Free will, memory, even the sense that your experience is continuous. All of it is a bit of a magic trick. So the childhood version of me wanted certainty, and the scientist version of me wants good questions. I'd say the questions got smaller in scope and bigger in depth. Instead of "what is the meaning of life?" I ask "why does this brain, right now, feel like it needs a meaning at all?" And that, to me, is a much more honest place to start.

r001.rationale: The response says neuroscience gave him better tools and changed the questions, but it explicitly says science did not answer the childhood questions. It does not describe becoming a scientist as beginning to answer questions he had previously dismissed as unanswerable.

astra-6.text:
I think science changes what you’re willing to accept as an answer. As a child, you ask, “Who am I? Why am I here? What happens when I die?” And you want an answer that makes the world feel understandable. As a scientist, you start asking, “How would I know if that answer were true? What could I measure? What would change my mind?”

Take “Who am I?” That’s a huge question. But you can study how memories contribute to your sense of self, or how a decision forms before you become aware of making it. You get a little piece of the answer, and often that piece makes the original question more complicated.

For me, that doesn’t take away the wonder. It makes the wonder more specific. You can understand something about how the brain works and still be astonished that this physical thing produces an experience of being you. You become more comfortable saying, “I don’t know,” while also seeing a way to find out a little more.

r001.rationale: The response says scientific methods can yield partial insight into big questions, but it does not communicate that these questions were previously dismissed as unanswerable in childhood.

sol-6.1.text:
I think science changes your relationship to the questions more than it necessarily gives you answers. As a child, you ask, “Who am I? Why am I here? What happens when I die?” And you expect that somewhere there’s an adult who knows. Then you grow up, become a scientist, and realize that we don’t know quite a lot.

But you gain a way of approaching that uncertainty. If I ask, “What is the self?” that’s an enormous question. If I ask, “Can I change your experience of being yourself by changing something in your brain?” now there’s something we can investigate.

To me, that doesn’t take away the wonder. It makes it more interesting. You can discover that an intuition you’ve had your entire life is wrong, and suddenly the question opens up again. So I think you keep the curiosity of the child, but become a little more careful about what you’re willing to call an answer.

r001.rationale: The response says becoming a scientist offers a way to investigate narrower questions, but it does not say this makes it possible to begin answering the childhood big questions previously dismissed as unanswerable.
